state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's clarify the concept of range. Range is the difference between the highest and lowest values in a set of data. If you change all values by the same proportion, the range will also change. Can you explain why you think Tom's or Katie's statement is correct in this scenario?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think I get what you're saying about the range being the difference between the highest and lowest values. But I'm still confused. If Tom cuts all the plants in half, wouldn't the highest and lowest just be smaller but still the same difference? And for Katie, if she adds \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) to each plant, wouldn't that just move everything up but keep the same range? Can you help me understand why that's not right?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's work through a brief example to clarify this. Let's say we have a set of data: \( 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 \). If we cut each value in half, the new set would be \( 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 \). The range of the original set is 8, while the range of the new set is 4. So changing all values by the same proportion does affect the range. Can you see how this applies to Tom and Katie's scenarios now?
